# Introduction

This is my codebook for the M01-1 workshop on literate programming with Quarto, following along with Dr. Jung, Dr. Lang, Jared, and Sena's presentation. I'm typing the code and syntax as they demonstrate it, organized into sections by topic so I can navigate back to any piece later.

# Project Setup in RStudio

Before writing any code, the workshop recommends starting a **New Project** in RStudio rather than just opening a loose file. This creates an `.Rproj` file automatically, and that `.Rproj` becomes the file to reopen next time (not the `.qmd` itself), because it sets the working directory for you automatically.

There are three ways to start a project:

- **New Directory** — creates a brand-new project folder on your local drive
- **Existing Directory** — turns a folder you already have into a project
- **Version Control (Git)** — clones a GitHub repository (e.g. cloning a class repo someone shares a URL for)

For this workshop, I used **New Directory \> Quarto Document/New Project** and created a `workshop1` folder to keep the `.qmd` file, its rendered output, and any images all in one place.

# Codebooks in R: Three Types

The workshop covered three different kinds of "codebooks" R users can work in:

1.  **R Script (`.R`)** — the original, simplest codebook. Everything typed is treated as code by default; you have to use `#` to mark something as a comment/note rather than code.
2.  **R Markdown (`.Rmd`)** — combines code, output, and prose in one document, but needs extra packages installed to unlock its full ecosystem (blogs, books, etc.).
3.  **Quarto (`.qmd`)** — the newer document type that does everything R Markdown can do without needing those extra packages, and also supports other languages (Python, Julia, Observable JS) and other IDEs (VS Code, Jupyter).

```{r}
#| eval: false
# This is what a comment looks like in an .R script — 
# everything else on an uncommented line is treated as code.
1 + 2
```

# The Three Areas of a Quarto Document

Every `.qmd` file is made up of three distinct areas:

1.  **YAML header** — bookended by three dashes (`---`) at the top and bottom. This determines the structure/settings of the rendered output (title, author, date, format, table of contents, etc.).
2.  **Code chunks** — started with three backticks and curly braces containing the language, e.g. ```` ```{r} ````, and closed with three backticks. Code goes here.
3.  **Text area** — everything outside of code chunks. This is where narrative/prose is written using Markdown syntax (headings, bold, links, etc.).

::: callout-note
The instructor's warning that stuck with me: don't write code in the text area — R Studio ignores it there unless it's inside a code chunk or written as special *inline code*. It might look fine while typing, but it will not evaluate when the document is rendered.
:::

## Reading Data the Base R Way vs. the Tidyverse Way

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Base R way - pass the data set into the function
head(mtcars)

# Tidyverse way - start with the data, then pipe into the function
mtcars |> head()
```

The Tidyverse's pipe-based (`|>`) style was introduced by Hadley Wickham (originally from New Zealand) around 2010, once R started being used heavily for data science rather than just statistics. It's a "mega package" of roughly ten packages, including `ggplot2`, that are designed to work together with a consistent grammar.

# Markdown Formatting Basics

## Headings

Headings are created with `#` symbols followed by a space — one `#` for a top-level heading, two for a sub-heading, and so on up to six levels deep. These automatically populate the document **Outline** panel in RStudio, which makes navigating a long `.qmd` file much easier.

``` markdown
# Hello
## My name is
### Jake
```

## Text Formatting

``` markdown
**this is bold**

`this is code`

*this is italicized*
```

In the visual editor, this can also be done by highlighting text and clicking the Bold / Italic / Code buttons in the toolbar — same result, different way of getting there.

## Lists

``` markdown
- item one
- item two
  - sub item
```

``` markdown
1. list one
2. list two
```

## Links and Images

``` markdown
[Google](https://google.com)
```

``` markdown
![Alt text describing the image](path-or-url-to-image.png)
```

Both of these can also be inserted visually — highlight text and use the link button, or use the image button, which opens a small file-browser/URL prompt.

## Callout Blocks and Block Quotes

Typing `/` opens Quarto's **Insert Anything** menu, which is the fastest way to insert callouts, block quotes, tables, figures, and even emojis without memorizing the raw syntax.

::: callout-note
This is a callout block, inserted using the `/` shortcut and selecting "Callout."
:::

> This is a block quote, also inserted using the `/` shortcut.

# Cross-Referencing a Table

To reference a table (or figure) elsewhere in the document, it needs a label that starts with `tbl-` (or `fig-` for figures) plus a caption. Referencing it later with `@tbl-example` creates a clickable link that pops up a preview of the table.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-example
#| tbl-cap: "This is a table"

data.frame(
  Column1 = c("A", "B", "C"),
  Column2 = c(1, 2, 3),
  Column3 = c("X", "Y", "Z")
)
```

See @tbl-example above for a simple three-column, three-row example.

# Controlling Code Visibility with Chunk Options

By default, Quarto shows both the code *and* its output when a document is rendered. The `echo` chunk option controls whether the code itself is displayed.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cars
#| fig-cap: "Speed vs. stopping distance in the built-in cars dataset"
#| echo: false

plot(cars)
```

Setting `echo: false` on this chunk means only the plot in @fig-cars shows up in the rendered document — the `plot(cars)` code itself is hidden. Flipping it to `echo: true` (or removing the option, since `true` is the default) would show the code above the plot as well.

# Output Formats

One of the biggest advantages of Quarto highlighted in the workshop is that the **same `.qmd` file** can render to multiple formats just by changing the YAML — no changes needed to the code or text itself:

- `html` — the default, web-ready output
- `pdf` — requires TinyTeX to be installed first
- `docx` — generates an actual Word document
- `revealjs` — turns the same content into an HTML slide presentation
- `pptx` — can even render out to PowerPoint format
- `dashboard` — for building interactive dashboards

A single document can also declare multiple formats at once in the YAML, and Quarto will generate all of them side by side (e.g. an HTML page with a downloadable PDF version of the same content).

# Publishing

Once a project is set up, Quarto can publish directly to the web with one command run in the RStudio **Terminal** tab:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
quarto publish
```

The workshop demonstrated publishing to **Netlify**, but Quarto also supports **Quarto Pub**, **GitHub Pages**, **Posit Connect**, and **Hugging Face**, most of which are free. This ties directly into the GitHub setup from earlier in the course — version control (Git) and publishing are two separate but connected pieces of the same reproducible workflow.
